A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ComfyUI workflow-generation research, renamed from GenAgent/OpenComfy to ComfyAgent/ComfyBench and substantially expanded. The main text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 20 OpenComfy tasks, representation ablations, repeated-run results, and generated examples.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations on 200 ComfyBench tasks, representation and component ablations, generated examples, and a human study validating its automated evaluator.

M1.justification: ComfyAgent retains GenAgent's memory and planning, combination, adaptation, retrieval, and refinement framework. The appendix prompts change the generation interface from separate node instantiation/invocation to one call per node, separate function and principle annotations, and discourage unrequested upscaling or interpolation. These are limited procedural refinements.

E1.justification: OpenComfy's 20 tasks become 200 tasks organized into vanilla, complex, and creative categories. Beyond increasing sample counts, v2 evaluates creative requirements that cannot be met by directly imitating or combining curriculum workflows, including identity-preserving transformations, relighting, and video-to-sketch conversion (Section 3.2 and supplementary Tables 6–7).

E2.justification: v1 compares GPT-4o-based zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and RAG agents. v2 retains these and adds evaluated CoT-SC and RAG comparators using Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama-3.1-70B, o1-mini, and o1-preview (Table 2), substantially broadening the comparison set.

E3.justification: v1 separately reports parsing and execution success at run and task levels. v2 reports execution pass rate and GPT-4o-judged instruction-satisfaction resolve rate by difficulty, introducing video-frame sampling and a 50-task human-validation protocol. Curriculum workflows increase from 12 to 20, and the representation ablation switches from GenAgent to GPT-4o with RAG.

E4.justification: v2 adds four component-removal ablations testing CombineAgent, AdaptAgent, RetrieveAgent, and RefineAgent, plus human validation of the automated judge. It revises the representation ablation, removes v1's pass@k analysis, and replaces the Budapest-video trajectory with an aquarium-video trajectory while expanding qualitative examples.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports five runs per benchmark task. v2 no longer documents that repetition scheme, but adds eight human judgments and eight GPT-4o judgments per question for 50 questions, averaged for Kendall, Pearson, and Spearman analyses with p-values (Table 1 and supplementary Section C). These statistics validate evaluator agreement; they do not establish increased benchmark repetitions.

E6.justification: v1 reports GenAgent execution success of 59% per run and 90% with any success across five runs. Under its different benchmark and metrics, v2 reports 56% pass, 32.5% resolve, and 15% creative-task resolve, alongside new model, ablation, and human-correlation results. These are not directly comparable performance changes. v2's GPT-4o RAG total resolve of 23% also conflicts with category scores implying approximately 28.5%.

T1.justification: Both versions retain the DAG description of workflows and the conceptual argument for code representation. Neither supplies formal theorems or proofs. v2's added evaluation metrics and correlation analyses do not introduce new theoretical derivations or formal properties.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds a general workflow-generation framework, superior execution success, and potential applicability toward AGI. v2 makes ComfyBench a principal contribution, claims comparable performance to o1-preview, and foregrounds only 15% success on creative tasks. This substantially revises the contribution emphasis and qualifies the earlier optimistic conclusions.

C2.justification: v2 adds model-specific hallucination explanations and interpretations of individual agents' roles from component ablations. It identifies creative generalization as a major unresolved challenge and explicitly discusses open-loop operation, excluded fine-tuning, omitted node-document inputs, and possible VLM-feedback refinement. These substantially expand v1's interpretation and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 specifies model snapshots, demonstration counts, the retrieval embedding model, documentation provenance, and automated-evaluation prompts and procedures that v1 did not document. It also revises agent templates and the worked trajectory. Documentation losses include the AnalyzeAgent template, the complete task listing, and the explicit project-page link; their removal does not establish that external resources became unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 positions ComfyBench as a first-of-its-kind benchmark and expands references to automated agent-system design, MindSearch, self-refinement, self-evolving agents, and contemporary models and visual components. It removes v1's explicit NCEN-QA/OpenAGI difficulty comparison and detailed CoRE critique, substantially revising how the contribution is situated relative to prior research.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the benchmark. v2 places a dedicated ComfyBench section before the method, condenses and reorganizes the workflow discussion, renames the framework and benchmark, and restructures the appendices from three sections into five.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a predominantly two-column layout, redraws the overview and architecture diagrams, and rearranges the representation illustration. It replaces large workflow-example figures with compact input/result tables, adds benchmark and human-validation displays, restructures evaluation tables by difficulty, and removes the pass@k plot.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness of v1's benchmark: successful execution did not establish that outputs satisfied instructions. The new resolve evaluation, checked against human judgments, substantially improves evaluation validity. Creative-generalization tests, broader comparisons, component ablations, and more qualified conclusions strengthen the paper further. These gains outweigh reduced repetition documentation and reporting problems, including inconsistent RAG totals and unexplained differences between Tables 2 and 3.
